description: Somos Sofia, Marilynn y Tomás, vamos a 4to año con especialidad en ciencias naturales, ciencias humanísticas y en informática. Estamos abiertos a sumar integrantes que puedan aportar lo necesario para formar un proyecto sólido.
summary:
Sembrando el Futuro is an application designed to advise and guide those who wish to get started in the world of cultivation.
It operates via an AI-powered virtual assistant (a chatbot-style interface) that continuously learns from the results and data the user records regarding their crops. Consequently, the platform provides personalized recommendations tailored to the user’s geographic location and local climate, specific soil conditions, and the individual goals of each grower.
details:
Project name

Sembrando el Futuro

Team name: XPerimental

Team members: Three

High-level project summary

Sembrando el Futuro is a web application designed to help people understand and manage the conditions that affect their crops. Our project focuses on challenges such as temperature stress, limited knowledge of crop rotation, possible pest-related symptoms, and the need to adapt agricultural practices to local conditions.

Our target audience includes people who are new to agriculture, beginner farmers, and experienced growers. The application combines environmental data from NASA POWER, a selected set of agricultural publications from Argentina’s National Institute of Agricultural Technology (INTA), and information provided by the user. An AI assistant helps explain the available information and suggests possible next steps in language adapted to the user’s experience.

We initially designed the prototype for Mendoza, Argentina. Our goal is to make environmental information easier to understand and use when planning or caring for crops. This is important because agricultural decisions depend on several connected factors, and beginners may not know which questions to ask or how to interpret regional climate data.

The application is a prototype and an educational decision-support tool. Its advice requires local verification and does not replace professional agronomic assessment.

What does the project do?

Sembrando el Futuro gives users a place to organize information about their growing areas and crops. Users can enter as guests or use a local demonstration account, create growing zones, add crops, and record observations.

The current prototype includes:

  • A crop-specific assistant that asks three questions about the user’s goal, the crop’s stage or planned planting date, growing conditions, soil, water, and available resources.
  • A general chatbot for broader agricultural questions.
  • Notes for recording observations about each crop.
  • A crop logbook where users can add tasks manually or generate a checklist from the conversation.
  • Reminders associated with individual crops.
  • A map showing the saved location of a growing zone when coordinates are available.
  • Links to satellite-based precipitation and soil-moisture visualizations.
  • A help guide and tutorial.

The assistant is designed to adapt its explanations to the user’s experience level. It is also instructed to distinguish known information from missing information and uncertainty.

How does it work?

The user creates a growing zone and can provide its latitude and longitude. They then add a crop and answer three initial questions. The application combines these answers with the information already saved for the zone, the crop, and the user’s notes.

When coordinates are available, the server requests daily environmental data from NASA POWER. The current request includes mean, minimum, and maximum air temperature; precipitation; relative humidity of the air; and modeled root-zone soil wetness. The application requests a historical period beginning in 1981 and prepares monthly summaries for the assistant while tracking available and missing daily values.

The server also provides Gemini with a small, prepared selection of findings from INTA publications. Gemini uses the supplied context to produce an explanation and possible next steps. It is instructed not to invent measurements, diagnoses, missing information, or access to sources that were not available.

For the crop logbook, the assistant can generate a checklist of pending activities mentioned in the conversation or notes. Users can also create and complete tasks themselves.

The current INTA component is not a live search of the entire INTA database. It is a limited selection of prepared summaries and may not contain specific evidence for every crop or location.

What factors did your team consider?

Our main considerations were:

  • Soil characteristics: Soil type and its ability to retain water can influence crop management. The application asks users what they know, but it cannot determine the capacity or fertility of an individual plot without additional evidence.
  • User experience: A beginner may need basic explanations and step-by-step guidance, while an experienced grower may prefer a more technical response.
  • Location: Climate conditions and suitable practices vary by place. The prototype initially focuses on Mendoza and can use saved coordinates to request regional data.
  • Crop rotation: Different crop sequences may affect soil management and future crops. The assistant considers rotation when relevant and when enough information is available.
  • Climate adaptation: Temperature, rainfall, and humidity provide context for discussing potential conditions affecting a crop.

We also considered water availability, irrigation methods, costs, tools, available time, and the user’s goals. These factors can limit which actions are practical.

What benefits does the project offer, and what do you hope to achieve?

We hope to give users a clearer starting point for managing their crops, especially when they are unsure what information matters or what to do next. The application brings together their own observations, regional environmental information, and selected agricultural guidance in one place.

For beginners, the main benefit is an accessible explanation of the factors to consider. For more experienced users, the application can serve as an organizational tool and provide additional regional context for their decisions.

In the future, we hope to expand and review the agricultural evidence available for different crops, improve the evaluation of crop rotation and climate adaptation, and connect reliable alert sources. We also aim to test the responses with concrete cases and agricultural specialists before presenting the system as a dependable source of operational advice.

At present, automatic weather alerts are not connected, and the application cannot confirm pests or diseases, determine exact irrigation requirements, or guarantee crop performance.

What NASA data and resources did you use?

NASA POWER

The application requests environmental data through the NASA POWER Daily API. The variables requested are:

  • Mean, minimum, and maximum air temperature.
  • Precipitation.
  • Relative humidity of the air.
  • Modeled root-zone soil wetness.

NASA POWER supplies regional environmental data derived from models and observations. Its meteorological products draw on sources such as NASA’s MERRA-2 assimilation model and more recent processing systems. These sources incorporate different observations, including satellite information.

The values should be understood as regional estimates rather than direct measurements of an individual farm or garden. The application distinguishes between humidity in the air and modeled moisture in the soil. Neither value alone establishes how much water is available to a particular plant or the exact amount of irrigation it needs.

NASA Worldview and Earth-observation layers

The application provides external links to NASA Worldview for visual exploration of IMERG precipitation, associated with the Global Precipitation Measurement mission, and SMAP Level 4 root-zone soil moisture.

Worldview uses NASA’s Global Imagery Browse Services to provide imagery for visualization. These maps are external visual resources. The precipitation visualization is not a local weather radar or an official alert, and the SMAP layer is not a direct measurement of the user’s plot.

The Worldview layers are separate from the POWER variables requested by the assistant. The application does not download those Worldview images for analysis by the chatbot.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed the prototype using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the web interface and application behavior; Node.js for server-side logic and API requests; the Google Gemini API for the assistant and checklist generation; the NASA POWER API for regional environmental data; and OpenStreetMap for the embedded location map.

We used Netlify and Netlify Functions for hosting and server-side functionality, Git and GitHub for version control and project hosting, Visual Studio Code as a development environment, and Canva and hand-drawn sketches for design planning.

The prototype does not require a dedicated sensor, satellite receiver, or other specialized hardware. Users access it through a device with a web browser and an internet connection.

Did you use AI tools? If so, how?

Yes. We used AI to support the development and presentation of our solution.

We used an AI coding assistant to help write, modify, troubleshoot, and test parts of the application. We also used AI to help organize and draft documentation, answer technical questions, and generate the XPerimental logo.

The prototype integrates Google Gemini to generate conversational explanations and checklists from the context supplied by the application.

The project concept and the sketches were developed by our team. The sketches were made by hand or in Canva. We did not use AI-generated audio or video.

Data, resources, and tools used

The project uses NASA POWER environmental data, NASA Worldview visualizations, the IMERG precipitation layer, the SMAP Level 4 root-zone soil-moisture layer, and NASA Global Imagery Browse Services.

For agricultural guidance, the application supplies Gemini with a limited selection of findings prepared from three INTA publications: Manual de la huerta agroecológica, La huerta orgánica, and Riego en cultivos hortícolas.

The project also uses the Google Gemini API, OpenStreetMap, Node.js, Netlify, Netlify Functions, Git, GitHub, Visual Studio Code, Canva, team-created sketches, and the AI-generated XPerimental logo.
